title: Blink: GPIO5 drives an LED
about: The classic first program. GPIO5 drives a red LED through a 220Ω resistor; a FreeRTOS task toggles the level every 500ms and prints the state over serial.

title: Button: toggle an LED with an interrupt
about: The on-board BOOT button is on GPIO9 (pulls to ground when pressed). A falling edge triggers a GPIO interrupt; the ISR sends a timestamp into a queue, and a task debounces it for 50ms before toggling the LED on GPIO5. Try pressing the BOOT button on the 3D board.

title: Breathing LED: LEDC hardware fade
about: LEDC outputs 5kHz, 13-bit PWM and uses the hardware fade to brighten and dim the LED. Note: the code says 1000ms, but IDF rounds the per-step increment down (8191÷5000→1), so on real hardware one fade actually takes about 1.64 seconds; the simulator reproduces this detail faithfully.

title: Servo: angle control with 50Hz PWM
about: SG90-style servos are driven by 50Hz PWM, where a 0.5–2.5ms pulse maps to 0–180°. GPIO6 steps through 0/45/90/135/180°.

title: Serial echo: UART send and receive
about: Installs the UART driver and reads the serial port byte by byte, echoing back each line it receives; type ping and it replies pong. Type in the serial box on the right and press Enter.

title: Hello World: chip info and timing
about: The ESP-IDF starter program: prints the chip model, revision, flash size and free heap, and uses esp_timer to measure how long vTaskDelay(500ms) actually takes.

title: Potentiometer: ADC sets brightness
about: The potentiometer wiper goes to GPIO2 (ADC1 channel 2, 12dB attenuation, range about 0–2.5V), and the reading is used directly as the PWM duty cycle of the LED on GPIO5. Drag the knob and watch the reading and brightness change together. ADC readings have ±2 LSB of noise, so they jitter slightly just like on real hardware.

title: RGB LED: on-board WS2812 (RMT)
about: The on-board addressable RGB LED is on GPIO8. ESP-IDF's led_strip component uses the RMT peripheral to send 24-bit colours with WS2812 timing (0.4µs high for 0, 0.8µs high for 1), cycling red, green, blue and white every 400ms. The simulator decodes the waveform on the pin back into colours.

title: OLED: text and graphics on an SSD1306
about: A 0.96-inch 128×64 OLED on I2C (address 0x3C, SDA=GPIO6, SCL=GPIO7, 400kHz). The program scans the bus, initialises the screen, then refreshes one frame per second: a title, two lines of text and a moving progress bar. Serial prints how long each frame's 1KB of display memory takes over I2C (about 24ms, matching real hardware).

title: Temperature, humidity and pressure: BME280 sensor
about: BME280 on I2C (address 0x76, SDA=GPIO6, SCL=GPIO7). The program reads the chip ID and factory calibration data, converts temperature, humidity and pressure using the datasheet formulas, and prints them once a second. Drag the sliders below to change the virtual environment and the readings follow.

title: DHT11 temperature / humidity: single-wire bit-bang (ESP32-C3)
about: A DHT11 module on GPIO5 (open drain, 10 kΩ pull-up on the module). The firmware's own driver pulls the line low for 20 ms, then times the sensor's answer by counting esp_rom_delay_us(1) loops: 80 µs low + 80 µs high, then 40 bits of 50 µs low followed by 27 µs (0) or 70 µs (1) high, ending with a checksum. It reads 100 times, one second apart, and prints how many passed the checksum. Drag the sliders to change the readings. Open the logic analyzer's fine sampling on GPIO5 to measure each bit with the cursors; the simulator also flags the busy-wait timing as needing a real-board check.

title: Thermo-hygrometer: BME280 + OLED (ESP32-C3)
about: Demo firmware for the board advisor's "thermo-hygrometer" project. A BME280 (0x76) and an SSD1306 OLED (0x3C) share one I2C bus: SDA=GPIO6, SCL=GPIO7 (D4 / D5 on the XIAO ESP32C3). Once a second it reads temperature, humidity and pressure, prints one line to serial and shows the same three lines on the OLED. Drag the sliders to change the virtual environment and the readings follow.

title: Round LCD: ESP32-C3 + GC9A01 (SPI2 + GDMA)
about: A 1.28-inch 240×240 GC9A01 round LCD on the C3's SPI2 (40MHz, data moved by GDMA): SCLK=GPIO6, MOSI=GPIO7, CS=GPIO10 (these three are SPI2's direct IO_MUX pins), DC=GPIO5, RST=GPIO4, backlight=GPIO3 (active high), VCC to 3.3V. The firmware first draws a full-screen test pattern of four coloured sectors plus a white ring, then moves a white ball around the circle with a partial refresh every 50ms. The C3's 400KB of SRAM can hold a full frame buffer (115KB).

title: Wi-Fi: scan nearby access points
about: A Wi-Fi station-mode scan that lists the 4 access points in the virtual world: SSID, channel, signal strength and security type. It uses the real ESP-IDF Wi-Fi driver; the simulator injects 802.11 beacons at the MAC register and DMA level.

title: Wi-Fi: connect and make HTTP requests
about: Joins the open access point TryBoard-WiFi, gets 192.168.4.100 from DHCP, then uses esp_http_client to request http://tryboard.local (mDNS) and example.com (DNS). The network is a virtual world inside the simulator and never touches the real internet. For an encrypted access point (WPA2-PSK), see the acceptance firmware wifi-wpa2.

title: NVS: a boot counter that survives power loss
about: The boot count is stored in the NVS partition in flash, incremented after every esp_restart, and stops at the third boot. The simulator's flash is really erased and written, and its contents survive a reset, just like a real board.

title: Arduino：Blink
about: Blink built with the Arduino IDE / arduino-cli (esp32 core 3.x); upload the exported merged.bin directly and it runs. LED on GPIO5.

title: Arduino: servo sweep with ESP32Servo
about: Built with arduino-cli and the ESP32Servo library (LGPL-2.1; the pinned library commit and build info ship with the bin). An SG90 on GPIO6 steps through 0/45/90/135/180° with 0.5–2.5 ms pulses at 50 Hz.

title: Arduino: send NEC IR codes with IRremote
about: Built with arduino-cli and the IRremote library (MIT). An IR LED on GPIO4 sends three NEC codes on a 38 kHz LEDC carrier; the serial log prints each command and the IR LED card shows what the eye decodes from the LED.

title: Arduino: MQTT publish / subscribe with PubSubClient
about: Built with arduino-cli and the PubSubClient library (MIT). Joins TryBoard-WiFi, connects to the virtual MQTT broker on port 1883, subscribes to tryboard/#, publishes tryboard/hello and prints every message it receives. Open the Network tab's MQTT view to publish your own message from the cloud.

title: IR remote receiver + transmitter on RMT (classic ESP32)
about: RMT RX on GPIO19 reads a VS1838B-class receiver, RMT TX on GPIO18 drives an IR LED with a 38 kHz carrier. At start the firmware sends one NEC frame (address 0x0440) that comes back through the receiver, then prints every key you press on the bench remote. The IR LED card shows the frames the eye decodes. Receiver timing uses typical values; not calibrated on real hardware.

title: Arduino: NEC IR sender on RMT, no library
about: Built with arduino-cli and the core's RMT API only. An IR LED on GPIO4 sends NEC frames (address 0xFF00, command 0xC936) on a 38 kHz RMT carrier; the IR LED card shows what the eye decodes from the LED.

title: Arduino: receive NEC IR codes with IRremote
about: Built with arduino-cli and the IRremote library (MIT), trimmed from its ReceiveDemo. A VS1838B-class receiver on GPIO5 is sampled by IRremote's 50 µs timer interrupt; press keys on the bench remote and the serial log prints the NEC address and command (repeat codes marked). Receiver timing uses typical values; not calibrated on real hardware.

title: Arduino: IR loopback, send and receive NEC on one board
about: Built with arduino-cli and the IRremote library (MIT). An IR LED on GPIO4 sends three NEC codes (address 0x10) on a 38 kHz LEDC carrier, and a VS1838B-class receiver on GPIO5, which the bench points the LED at, decodes each one back; the serial log prints both ends and the IR LED card shows what the eye sees. Same-bench light path only, no distance or angle; not calibrated on real hardware.

title: S3 native USB: become a keyboard + mouse
about: The ESP32-S3 uses its built-in USB OTG (TinyUSB) to present itself as a HID keyboard + mouse: 1 second after being plugged into a computer it types a line of text and draws a square with the mouse, then repeats each time you press BOOT. The virtual computer on the left goes through full enumeration (get descriptors, set address, read the report descriptor) and turns the received keystrokes back into text. The USB port on the C3 / C6 can only act as a serial port, so they can't do this.

title: S3 native USB: virtual serial port (CDC-ACM)
about: The ESP32-S3 uses native USB to provide a CDC-ACM virtual serial port: a new COM port / ttyACM appears on the computer, with no USB-to-serial chip in between. Type a line in the "USB serial terminal" below and the board sends it back in upper case.

title: Blink (S3): GPIO5 drives an LED
about: The same source as the C3 version, on an ESP32-S3 dev board instead (N16R8: 16MB flash + 8MB PSRAM, dual core). GPIO5 drives an LED through 220Ω and toggles every 500ms.

title: On-board RGB (S3): WS2812 on GPIO48
about: The S3 dev board's on-board RGB LED is on GPIO48 (some newer boards moved it to GPIO38). The RMT peripheral sends data with WS2812 timing, cycling red → green → blue → white.

title: OLED (S3): SSD1306
about: A 0.96-inch 128×64 OLED on I2C (address 0x3C, SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9, 400kHz). Same source as the C3 version, only the pins changed.

title: Potentiometer (S3): ADC sets brightness
about: The potentiometer wiper goes to GPIO4 (ADC1 channel 3, 12dB attenuation, range about 0–3.1V), and the reading is used as the PWM duty cycle of the LED on GPIO5. Unlike the C3, single-shot sampling on the S3 goes through the RTC SENS controller, but the firmware code needs no changes.

title: Dual core (S3): tasks pinned to both cores
about: Two tasks are pinned to core 0 / core 1; each adds 20,000 to a spinlock-protected counter, they pass messages across cores through a queue, and then esp_ipc makes core 1 run a function. A correct count shows that interleaved execution on both cores and the atomic operations all work.

title: Inclinometer: MPU6050 6-axis (I2C)
about: A GY-521 (MPU6050, I2C 0x68) lies flat on the breadboard: SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9, VCC to 3.3V. The firmware uses ESP-IDF's i2c_master driver to access registers (WHO_AM_I, reset, wake from sleep, 100 Hz sampling, ±2 g / ±250 °/s), prints acceleration, gyro and temperature every 200ms, and computes pitch and roll from the gravity components: roll = atan2(ay, az), pitch = atan2(−ax, √(ay²+az²)). Drag the tilt sliders below, or press and drag the module in 3D to rotate the whole table, and the readings follow; while rotating, the gyro reads angular velocity.

title: Inclinometer: QMI8658 6-axis (I2C)
about: QMI8658 (I2C 0x6B, the one on the Waveshare round-display board): SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9. Same source as the MPU6050 version, switched to the QMI8658 registers: soft reset, CTRL1 enables address auto-increment (without it a burst read keeps reading the same register, a common trap on real hardware), ±4 g / ±512 °/s, CTRL7 enables the accelerometer and gyro; data is little-endian. Drag the tilt sliders to see pitch, roll and gyro readings.

title: Touch round LCD: GC9A01 + CST816S, draw where you tap
about: A 1.28-inch touch round LCD (like the Waveshare 1.28inch Touch LCD: GC9A01 display + CST816S capacitive touch). The display uses SPI2 (SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight=GPIO15); touch uses I2C 0x15: TP_SDA=GPIO6, TP_SCL=GPIO7, TP_INT=GPIO5 (pulled low while touched), TP_RST=GPIO16. A falling-edge interrupt on INT wakes a task, which reads coordinates and draws a dot every 20ms while touched, then reads the gesture on release (tap / swipe / long press for 1 second clears the screen). Tap and drag directly on the round screen in 3D.

title: 2.16″ AMOLED: CO5300 over QSPI, four-quadrant test picture
about: The Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-2.16 all-in-one board: a 480×480 AMOLED driven by a CO5300 over quad SPI (CS=GPIO12, CLK=GPIO38, D0–D3=GPIO4–7, RST=GPIO39) through esp_lcd and the esp_lcd_co5300 component. The firmware draws red / green / blue quadrants and a grey ramp in the bottom-right in 40-row strips, then prints a pixel checksum and how long the bus took. The picture appears on the square screen of the 3D board.

title: 2.16″ AMOLED board: touch, battery, PWR key and RTC on one I2C bus
about: Same Waveshare AMOLED board, now its I2C bus (SDA=GPIO15, SCL=GPIO14): CST9220 touch (0x5A, INT=GPIO11, RST=GPIO40), AXP2101 power management (0x34), PCF85063 RTC (0x51) and the ES8311 / ES7210 audio codecs (0x18 / 0x40). It reads every chip ID and the battery state, sets the RTC and reads it back 3 s later, then prints touches and AXP2101 events. Tap the 3D screen for TOUCH lines; in the board panel drag the battery slider, plug or unplug USB and press PWR (short / long). The audio codecs only answer ID reads: no sound is simulated.

title: AI gateway dashboard: Claude Desktop heartbeats on the 2.16″ AMOLED
about: The Waveshare AMOLED board as a desk buddy for Claude Desktop. The firmware (LVGL, NimBLE, advertising as Claude-Dash) takes heartbeat JSON lines over the Nordic UART service and draws four pages on the 480×480 screen: requests (sessions running / waiting), context, sessions and usage (tokens, battery, RTC clock). Swipe left or right on the screen to change pages. The virtual PC in the "Bluetooth" tab of the bottom dock is already on: it finds the board, sets the time and sends a heartbeat every few seconds; edit the numbers there and send to watch the screen change. Battery and USB come from the board panel. The BLE link is a behaviour model; range and pairing need real hardware.

title: Desk weather station: temperature + screen + dial
about: An assembled ESP32-S3 build. A BME280 and an SSD1306 share one I2C bus (SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9) and are read every 500ms: the OLED shows the temperature in large digits with humidity and pressure on the line below; a servo on GPIO4 acts as a needle dial (0–40℃ → 0.5–2.5ms); the on-board RGB (GPIO48) is blue below 18℃, green below 28℃ and red otherwise. Press BOOT (GPIO0) to switch between ℃ / ℉. At ≥ 30℃ the passive buzzer on GPIO5 sounds an alarm (2.7kHz, 200ms on, 200ms off, stopping once below 29℃; sound only plays after you click "Sound" in the toolbar). An LED (through 220Ω) is also wired in parallel on GPIO5 for checkpoints 01 / 02. Drag the environment sliders and watch all three change together.

title: LVGL dial: round-screen animation and frame rate
about: ESP32-S3 + GC9A01 round LCD (240×240, SPI2 40MHz + GDMA; SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight=GPIO15). The firmware uses LVGL 9.2 + esp_lvgl_port: a scale, a needle, a value label and an animated arc going round, with a 16ms refresh period (target 60 FPS) and two 40-line DMA buffers. The arc moves every frame, so almost the whole screen is redrawn and the CPU runs flat out: a stress test for round-screen UIs. Serial prints the FPS once a second (frames per second of simulated time, about 33; estimated 20–30 on real hardware at 160MHz). The multiplier at the top right of the page is the simulation speed: this example can't run in real time in the browser (about 0.5× in desktop browsers, depending on the machine), so the animation looks slow, but the frame rate is counted in simulated time and is unaffected.

title: Lens buddy: a pair of eyes on a round screen
about: An assembled ESP32-S3 build. GC9A01 round LCD (240×240, SPI2): SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight=GPIO15 (active high), VCC to 3.3V. The firmware uses ESP-IDF's esp_lcd + the espressif/esp_lcd_gc9a01 driver (SPI 40MHz, GDMA transfers) to draw a pair of cyan rounded-rectangle eyes with white highlights and pink blush, blinking every 3 seconds. Press BOOT (GPIO0) to switch moods: normal → happy → love → sleepy, and serial prints lines like MOOD 1 happy.

title: Little Yellow who turns around: servo turntable + round-screen face
about: An assembled ESP32-S3 build. The servo signal is on GPIO4 (LEDC 50Hz) and swings ±60° around 90°, one round trip every 2 seconds (pulse width 1.5 ± 0.667ms). GC9A01 round LCD (240×240, SPI2): SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight=GPIO15 (active high), VCC to 3.3V. The screen shows Little Little Yellow's face, with its eyes looking in the direction of rotation. Press BOOT (GPIO0) to stop it facing front (90°) and print LOOK FRONT; press again to resume turning.

title: Servo moves, board resets: a USB-power brownout demo
about: ESP32-S3 with an SG90 on GPIO4, reversing between 0° ↔ 180° every 150 ms (it always reverses mid-travel, where current peaks). Powered only from the computer's USB (current-limited to about 0.5 A), the servo drags down the 5V rail and 3V3 falls below 2.44 V → brownout reset, and serial shows rst:0xf (BROWNOUT_RST) and BOOT n reason=BROWNOUT. Switch the power supply to an external 5 V 2 A and it no longer resets; after 12 full sweeps it prints TRYBOARD_OK.

title: Wi-Fi (S3): scan nearby access points
about: Same source as the C3 version, targeting the ESP32-S3 instead (dual core, Wi-Fi task on core 0). The real ESP-IDF Wi-Fi driver scans the 4 access points in the virtual world; the S3 and C3 Wi-Fi MACs are the same hardware generation, so the simulator shares one MAC model.

title: Wi-Fi (S3): connect and make HTTP requests
about: Same source as the C3 version: joins the open access point TryBoard-WiFi, gets 192.168.4.100 from DHCP, then requests http://tryboard.local (mDNS) and example.com (DNS). The network is a virtual world inside the simulator and never touches the real internet; transmit current from the S3 datasheet (802.11b 21 dBm, about 340 mA) is counted in the power budget.

title: USB keypad: 4 keys + a macro key
about: The ESP32-S3 uses native USB (TinyUSB) to present itself as a HID keyboard named TryBoard Macro Pad. Four tactile buttons on the breadboard go to GPIO4 / 5 / 6 / 7 (other side to ground, internal pull-ups): K1–K3 send a / b / c, and K4 is a macro key that types Hello TryBoard followed by a newline. The virtual computer on the left goes through enumeration and turns the received keystrokes back into text. Click the keycaps in 3D to try it.

title: Rotary encoder: PCNT quadrature counting
about: An EC11 rotary encoder (KY-040 module) with CLK on GPIO6, DT on GPIO7 and the push button on GPIO15. The S3's PCNT uses two channels with each other's signal as edge / level for 4x quadrature counting (4 counts per detent); limits are set to ±100, and overflow is accumulated by the driver. Drag or scroll the knob in 3D and serial prints the count; press and hold the knob to print SW DOWN.

title: Ultrasonic ranging: HC-SR04 + RMT receive
about: The HC-SR04 runs on 5 V, with Trig on GPIO17 (GPIO sends a 10 µs pulse) and Echo through a 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider to GPIO18, where an RMT receive channel records the high-pulse width at 1 MHz resolution and converts it to distance (343 m/s). Drag the obstacle in front of the sensor in 3D and the distance on serial follows.

title: I2S playback: 440 Hz on a MAX98357A speaker
about: The ESP32-S3's I2S0 uses standard Philips format (44.1 kHz, 16-bit, mono duplicated to left and right) and GDMA to send a 440 Hz sine wave to a MAX98357A amplifier (BCLK=GPIO16, LRC=GPIO17, DIN=GPIO18) driving a small 4Ω speaker. i2s_channel_write is throttled at playback speed by the DMA EOF interrupt, so the write rate on serial matches the sample rate exactly. Click "Sound" in the toolbar to listen; the panel also shows the PCM readings received by the simulator and the dominant frequency measured at the web page's output.

title: I2S recording: RMS and frequency from an INMP441 mic
about: The ESP32-S3's I2S1 reads an INMP441 digital microphone at 16 kHz with 32-bit slots on the left channel (SCK=GPIO39, WS=GPIO40, SD=GPIO41, L/R to ground), computing and printing RMS and zero-crossing frequency every 1024 samples. By default the mic hears a 1 kHz test WAV (synthesised by us, sampled in simulated time, so results are identical every run); in the panel you can switch to a sweep, silence, or, after granting permission, the browser microphone (for fun only, not part of acceptance).

title: Voice assistant (xiaozhi-protocol compatible)
about: An ESP32-S3 voice assistant that speaks the open xiaozhi WebSocket protocol to a virtual server inside the simulator (never the real xiaozhi.me): INMP441 mic on SCK=GPIO5, WS=GPIO4, SD=GPIO6, MAX98357A speaker on BCLK=GPIO15, LRC=GPIO16, DIN=GPIO7, SSD1306 OLED on SDA=GPIO41, SCL=GPIO42. Hold BOOT (in 3D or the Voice tab) to talk: the mic streams a recorded clip as Opus-sized frames, the server answers with what it heard and a spoken reply, the speaker plays it and the OLED shows the subtitle. Tap BOOT while it speaks to interrupt. The voice link is a behavioural model; wake word and echo cancellation need real hardware.

title: Knob lamp: EC11 knob + WS2812 strip
about: An assembled ESP32-S3 build. An 8-LED WS2812 strip with DIN on GPIO5 (RMT transmit, level-shifted to 5 V by a 74AHCT125, strip powered from an external 5 V), and an EC11 encoder with CLK=GPIO6, DT=GPIO7, SW=GPIO15 on PCNT (4x, 4 counts per detent). On power-up it lights the LEDs warm white one by one; turn the knob to adjust brightness (8 levels), press once to switch to changing colour (6 colours), press again to go back to brightness. Drag or scroll the knob in 3D; clicking it presses it.

title: Ultrasonic ruler: HC-SR04 + OLED + buzzer
about: An assembled ESP32-S3 build. HC-SR04 (5 V) with Trig=GPIO17 and Echo through a 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider to GPIO18; RMT receive measures the echo width once every 100 ms. An SSD1306 (0x3C, SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9) shows the distance in large digits plus a distance bar; the passive buzzer on GPIO5 works like a parking sensor: within 1 m it beeps for 40 ms and pauses distance×5 ms, and within 10 cm it sounds continuously (sound only plays after you click "Sound"). Drag the obstacle in 3D.

title: Tilt buddy: QMI8658 + round screen
about: An assembled ESP32-S3 build. A QMI8658 6-axis IMU (I2C 0x6B, SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9) reads the orientation every 20 ms; on the GC9A01 round LCD (SPI2: SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight=GPIO15) a little bean slides in the direction of tilt and slides along the edge when it hits the rim. Drag the tilt sliders, or press and drag the IMU module in 3D to rotate the whole table.

title: Bluetooth heart-rate strap: NimBLE peripheral + virtual phone
about: A NimBLE peripheral: advertises TryBoard-HR and provides heart rate (one notification per second once subscribed), battery level (87%) and an LED switch characteristic (write 01 to light the LED on GPIO5). Choose "Virtual phone" to scan, connect, read, subscribe and write; the "Bluetooth" tab in the bottom dock lists every packet in the air in simulated time. The protocol is a behaviour model; signal range, walls and differences between phone OSes must be checked on real hardware.

title: Hello World (classic ESP32)
about: The same hello_world on the classic ESP32 (dual-core Xtensa LX6, ESP32-DevKitC V4): prints the chip model, core count, flash size and free heap.

title: Blink (classic ESP32): GPIO2 drives an LED
about: Same source as the C3 version. The ESP32-DevKitC V4 only has a power LED and no user LED, so an external LED is wired to GPIO2 (through 220Ω) and toggles every 500ms.

title: Wi-Fi 配网：板子开热点，手机填密码
about: 板子先开开放热点 TryBoard-Setup，并把所有网址都指向自己（DNS 劫持），手机连上就弹出「需要登录」的配网页。在底部「网络」页签里用虚拟手机连热点、打开登录页、填家里 Wi-Fi（虚拟路由器 MyHome / 12345678）并提交：板子存进 NVS、关热点去连路由器，之后自己重启一次，从 NVS 读出配置直接连上。手机弹不弹登录页因机型而异，要上真机确认。

title: Wi-Fi：真实网络开关（HTTP）
about: 先请求虚拟服务器 tryboard.local，再请求 example.com 和 httpbin.org/get。默认只连虚拟网络（结果可复现）；打开顶栏「真实网络」后，这两个请求经浏览器真的发出去：example.com 不给跨域头，会显示「浏览器没放行，原因 cors」；httpbin.org 允许跨域，拿到真实回复。只放行 HTTP，回复进输入日志，可离线重放。

title: Resilient weather station: survives router reboots and DNS failures
about: Joins TryBoard-WiFi and polls http://api.weather.example every 2 s. Try the presets in the Network tab (weak signal, flaky, offline) or schedule a router reboot, a DNS failure or a silent server: the firmware prints the disconnect reason, reconnects on its own and says when requests succeed again. Faults run on simulated time with a fixed seed, go into the input log and replay with tryboard run --inputs. Real routers and ISPs fail in more ways; check on real hardware.

title: Wi-Fi（经典 ESP32）：联网发 HTTP 请求
about: 与 C3 版同一份源码：连上开放热点 TryBoard-WiFi，DHCP 拿到 192.168.4.100，再请求 http://tryboard.local（mDNS）和 example.com（DNS）。经典 ESP32 的 Wi-Fi MAC 是上一代硬件（寄存器在 0x3FF73000 一带），模拟器用同一个 MAC 模型换一套寄存器排布；网络是虚拟世界，不会访问真实互联网。

title: Cheap Yellow Display: 2.8″ ILI9341 screen and XPT2046 touch
about: ESP32-2432S028 ("Cheap Yellow Display"): an ILI9341 240×320 panel on HSPI (SCLK=GPIO14, MOSI=GPIO13, CS=GPIO15, DC=GPIO2, backlight GPIO21) and an XPT2046 resistive touch controller on VSPI (CLK=GPIO25, DIN=GPIO32, DOUT=GPIO39, CS=GPIO33, PENIRQ=GPIO36). It draws colour bands with a yellow marker in the top-left corner, then waits for a touch: tap the 3D screen and it prints the raw reading and the pixel it maps to. The touch calibration span is estimated, not measured on a real board. The RGB LED, light sensor, speaker and SD slot are not simulated.

title: DS18B20 waterproof probes: 1-Wire bus, ROM search (ESP32-C3)
about: Two DS18B20 probes share one 1-Wire bus on GPIO4 (4.7 kΩ pull-up to 3V3). The firmware's own bit-bang driver sends a reset, finds both 64-bit ROM codes with the search algorithm, checks the power mode and reads each probe once a second (750 ms 12-bit conversion). Drag the temperature slider: probe 2 reads 0.5 ℃ higher than probe 1. Open the logic analyzer on GPIO4 to see the reset / presence pulses and the time slots.

title: Night light: PIR motion + light sensor drive a relay (ESP32-C3)
about: An HC-SR501 PIR on GPIO4, a photoresistor divider on GPIO3 (ADC) and a 5 V relay module on GPIO5. The relay closes only when it is dark and someone moves, and opens again once the PIR output drops. Set the light to Night, then press Wave on the PIR card: the relay LED lights and the serial log prints how long it stayed closed. The run ends after 11 s with a summary line.

title: RC522 RFID reader: read card UIDs over SPI (ESP32-C3)
about: An MFRC522 reader on SPI2 (SCK GPIO4, MOSI GPIO6, MISO GPIO5, SDA / CS GPIO7, RST GPIO3). The firmware reads the chip version, turns the antenna on and polls for cards: REQA, anticollision and SELECT, then prints the UID, SAK and ATQA. Tap a card on the RC522 card (a 4-byte and a 7-byte UID) and take it away again. MIFARE authentication and block reads are not modelled.

title: RFID door lock: RC522 + relay + SH1106 OLED (ESP32-C3)
about: An assembled ESP32-C3 build. An RC522 reader on SPI2 (SCK GPIO4, MOSI GPIO6, MISO GPIO5, SDA / CS GPIO7, RST GPIO3) polls for cards; a 1.3″ SH1106 OLED (0x3C, SDA GPIO2, SCL GPIO9) shows WELCOME, DENIED or the lockout countdown. The whitelisted card DE:AD:BE:EF closes the relay on GPIO10 (the door strike) for 3 s with a short beep on GPIO1; any other card gets a long beep and three red LED blinks on GPIO0, and three refusals in a row lock the reader for 10 s. Tap the whitelisted or the unknown card, then take it away.

title: IR remote night light: VS1838B + WS2812 strip
about: An assembled ESP32-S3 build. A VS1838B-class IR receiver with OUT on GPIO4 is read by RMT receive (1 MHz) and decoded as NEC; the 8-LED WS2812 strip from the knob lamp has DIN on GPIO5 (RMT transmit, level-shifted to 5 V by a 74AHCT125, strip powered from an external 5 V). The common 21-key NEC remote (address 0x00) drives it: digits 1–9 (0x0C 0x18 0x5E 0x08 0x1C 0x5A 0x42 0x52 0x4A) pick red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, purple, pink, warm white, white; VOL+ (0x15) / VOL- (0x07) step brightness through 8 levels, and holding them sends repeat codes that keep ramping; CH- (0x45, the power key on remotes that label it so) switches the light on and off. Serial prints every code, the new state and a strip current estimate (1 mA idle per LED + 20 mA per colour channel at full: about 488 mA at full white, an estimate, not measured). Press keys on the bench remote.

title: Temperature and humidity to the cloud: AHT20 + Wi-Fi + MQTT (ESP32-C3)
about: An ESP32-C3 reads an AHT20 on I2C (SDA GPIO6, SCL GPIO7, 0x38), joins TryBoard-WiFi and connects with ESP-IDF esp-mqtt to the virtual broker at mqtt://192.168.4.1:1883. Every 5 s it publishes {"t":23.5,"h":45.0,"seq":N} to tryboard/cloud/data. Publish interval=<1–60> to tryboard/cloud/cmd to change the period; the board acknowledges on tryboard/cloud/ack and refuses anything else. The broker and network are virtual: real Wi-Fi range, broker login and TLS need real hardware.

title: Temperature screen: DS18B20 on a 2.4″ ILI9341 colour TFT (ESP32-C3)
about: A bare 2.4″ ILI9341 module on the fixed SPI2 LCD pins (SCLK GPIO6, MOSI GPIO7, CS GPIO10, DC GPIO5, RST GPIO4, backlight GPIO3) and a DS18B20 probe on GPIO1 (GPIO4 is taken by the screen reset). The firmware reads the probe four times a second with its own 1-Wire driver and redraws the 240×320 screen only when the reading changes: big seven-segment digits, blue below 15 ℃, green, red above 28 ℃, and a −10…40 ℃ bar. Drag the temperature slider to watch the screen follow.

title: Motion monitor: PIR on a 1.3″ SH1106 OLED (ESP32-C3)
about: A 1.3″ SH1106 OLED on I2C (0x3C, SDA GPIO6, SCL GPIO7) and an HC-SR501 PIR on GPIO4. The SH1106 has 132 columns of memory with the glass starting at column 2, so the firmware sends each page from column 2 (an SSD1306 driver would shift the picture). Press Wave on the PIR card: the screen flips to an inverted MOTION banner, counts visits and shows how long the last one lasted; the serial log prints each edge.

title: Three I2C breakouts on one bus: AHT20, INA219, DS3231 (ESP32-C3)
about: An AHT20 temperature / humidity sensor (0x38), an INA219 current monitor (0x40) and a ZS-042 DS3231 clock (0x68) share one I2C bus on SDA GPIO6 / SCL GPIO7. The firmware scans the bus, checks each chip four times (AHT20 CRC, INA219 shunt and current registers agree, the DS3231 clock ticks and alarm 1 fires), then prints a live line every second. Drag the temperature slider: the AHT20 and the DS3231's own thermometer follow it. The INA219 reads the board's USB 5 V rail and the current the electrical model estimates.

title: Dial timer: M5Stack Dial ring, button, touch and buzzer (Arduino)
about: The M5Stack Dial as a kitchen timer, Arduino + M5Unified. Turn the ring to set 1–60 minutes (encoder on G40 / G41 read by the pulse counter), press the Dial (BtnA, G42) to start or pause, and the round GC9A01 screen counts down with a ring that shrinks as time runs out. At zero the buzzer on G3 beeps three times at 2 kHz (M5Unified Speaker, 1-bit audio over I2S); tap the screen to cancel a running countdown. Serial prints every setting, the remaining time each second and every beep. The countdown follows simulated time; buzzer loudness is not calibrated on real hardware.

title: AMOLED desk clock: RTC face, battery page, set the time from the phone
about: The Waveshare 2.16″ AMOLED board as a desk clock, nothing to wire. LVGL draws HH:MM as large seven-segment digits from the PCF85063 RTC (seconds below, refreshed in place); swipe left or right for the chip temperature page (the S3's internal sensor, which reads the die, not the room) and the battery page (AXP2101 level, USB and charging, VBAT). A short press of the PWR key blanks the AMOLED (brightness 0x51 = 0) and wakes it again. Over BLE (NimBLE, advertising as TryBoard-Clock) a phone writes 4-byte little-endian epoch seconds to characteristic FF11 to set the RTC. Battery and USB come from the board panel. The BLE link is a behaviour model; range and pairing need real hardware.
